opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came from watching what people were actually trying to build. Over the last couple of years we saw teams move from simple chatbots to agents that take actions: querying data, updating records, kicking off workflows. Almost every one of them hit the same wall. The agent's "world" was scattered across a dozen systems. There was an operational database for the app, a warehouse or lakehouse for analytics, a vector store for retrieval, some key-value cache for memory, and a separate place for logs and traces. Each one had its own permissions model, its own copy of the data, and its own notion of freshness.

For a human engineer that's annoying but manageable, because you learn the quirks. For an agent it's really problematic. The agent doesn't know that the vector index is six hours stale, or that the customer table in the warehouse is a nightly snapshot of the one in Postgres. So you get agents that reason correctly over the wrong data, which is in some ways worse than a crash.

So the first insight was that a lot of agent reliability is really a data problem. If the transactional data, the analytical history, the embeddings, and the agent's own state and memory all live in one governed storage layer, with one set of access controls and lineage, a whole class of failures goes away. The agent sees a consistent view. You can audit what it read and what it wrote. And you can answer "why did it do that?" by looking at one place instead of stitching together five systems.

The second piece is that agents behave very differently from human users of a database. They spin up lots of short-lived work. They want to branch: "let me try this change in a sandbox copy, check the result, then commit or throw it away." They generate huge numbers of small queries. Traditional databases weren't designed for that pattern, and separating storage from compute on open formats makes it much cheaper to give every agent its own branch or ephemeral instance on top of the same underlying data.

The third piece is the feedback loop. The data an agent produces, like its actions, outcomes, and evaluations, is exactly what you need to improve it. If that lands in the same place as your business data, you can evaluate, fine-tune, and monitor without a big ETL project. That closes the loop between running agents and making them better, which I think is where a lot of the real value will come from.

So it wasn't one moment. It was seeing the same pain point repeated across many customers, and realizing that the lakehouse ideas we'd been pushing for analytics, like one copy of the data, open formats, and unified governance, apply even more strongly when the consumer of the data is an AI system rather than a person.

r001.rationale: The response says agents benefit from access to unified business and operational data, but it does not connect that access to investigating SLA dips or distinguish it from service and database telemetry.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from watching what people were actually building on top of Databricks once agents started showing up in production. The pattern was almost always the same: you'd have the "real" data sitting in a lakehouse, and then around it a growing constellation of little side systems. A vector database over here for retrieval. A key-value store for agent memory or conversation state. Some Postgres instance that the application team spun up because the agent needed to write things back transactionally. Maybe a feature store or a cache in front of all that. And every one of those boundaries was a place where governance broke, where data got stale, where someone had to write a sync job, and where the agent would confidently reason over a snapshot that was three hours old.

What really convinced me, though, was looking at how agents differ from the previous generation of applications. A traditional app has a human in the loop deciding what to query. An agent is deciding on its own, at runtime, which data to pull, often across modalities: it wants to run a SQL aggregation, then do a semantic search over documents, then look up some structured record about a customer, then write an intermediate result back so another agent or a later step can use it. If each of those lives in a different system with a different access model, you either give the agent far too much access, or you spend all your time building glue. Neither is great. The failure mode we kept seeing was that the agent itself was fine, but the plumbing around it was fragile and nobody trusted the output because nobody could trace where the data came from.

And there's a cost dimension that people underestimate. Operational databases were designed around the assumption that a small number of humans or services are issuing requests. Agents change that economics completely. They issue a lot of exploratory queries, they spin up ephemeral state, and increasingly they want to create a whole scratch environment, test something, and throw it away. That looks much more like how we think about compute and storage in the lakehouse world, with separation of storage and compute and cheap branching, than like a classic monolithic OLTP box you provision for peak load and babysit forever.

So the thesis became: if you can have one storage layer with one catalog, one set of permissions, one lineage story, and you can serve both the analytical and the transactional and the retrieval workloads off it, then the agent gets a single coherent view of the world and the people responsible for the data get a single place to govern it. That felt less like a nice-to-have and more like a prerequisite for actually trusting agents with anything important. Once we started prototyping it internally and saw how much of the glue code just disappeared, that was the point where I stopped thinking of it as a research idea and started thinking of it as something we had to ship.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents accessing varied lakehouse, document, and customer data, but does not connect that access to investigating SLA dips or distinguish underlying business data from service and database telemetry.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that an agent’s task usually doesn’t fit neatly into one kind of database query. It might need to search some documents, look up a customer’s records, and then analyze what’s changed over time. Those are all parts of answering one question, but we’ve often put the data in separate systems.

If you unify the underlying storage, you can give the agent different ways to access the same data without making it reconcile a bunch of copies. That makes it easier to keep the information consistent and apply the same access controls. To me, that’s the compelling part: the agent can choose the right way to retrieve information for each step, while working from a common source of truth.

r001.rationale: The response mentions documents, customer records, and changing data, but does not identify access to business data beyond service and database telemetry as helping agents investigate SLA dips.

sol-6.1.text:
What convinced me was thinking about the access patterns of an agent. It might start with a semantic search to find relevant documents, then look up a customer record, then run a SQL query to check some numbers. Those are all steps in answering one question, but traditionally they involve separate systems, each with its own copy of the data.

That creates a lot of complexity. Are the copies up to date? Do they have the same permissions? Can you combine the results reliably? For an agent, those issues directly affect whether it gets the right answer.

So the appeal of unified storage is that you can support those different ways of accessing the same underlying data. You still need specialized indexes and execution techniques, but you can share the work of keeping the data fresh, governing it, and making it available. Agents make that combination especially useful because they move between these access patterns dynamically.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents combining semantic search, customer records, and SQL over shared data, but it does not connect this to investigating SLA dips or distinguish business data from service and database telemetry.
